The grasslands are. collectively owned. That's what was called the commons. And they still exist today also, for example, in Africa and many places. So it's a very commonly known thing. There's a tension between your individual behavior and profits. the collective interests, because if you let your cows eat the grass or let your sheep eat the grass, then another person cannot do it anymore. And there is a second thing, and that was actually a main point by Harden. It's a short-term depletion of resources versus long-term sustainability of the resource in general. And what he says, actually, the reception of his article is basically that it's a kind of definitive argument against commons arrangements. So the idea that you cannot have commons, it's only either the state or markets and private property comes from that article. And that's because commons are simply impossible. So if you want to have decent arrangements, it's... one or the other. And the reception is that the one focusing on the need for private property, which is also what you do in your article, and market clearing and price mechanism. And there he says that is not solved by private property or price mechanism. That's only solved by heavy state intervention. Mutual coercion. There's a phrase in his article or heading, the freedom to breed is intolerable. And in fact, he turned out to be in favor of China's one child per family policy. But the article has been taken as a definitive argument against Commons. Now, this is a long time ago, and what is less known is that there is a whole empirical literature on commons that also extends these days to Internet and web and other forms of digital. Eleanor Ostrom, a political scientist at Indiana University, basically spent her life, I think she died, three or four years ago, something like that. She has been analyzing lots and lots of local commons that exist and are failures and are successes. For example, define clear boundaries, who is entitled to be involved in the use of the resources. Make sure that there is a deliberation. that make sure that there are conflict resolution mechanisms, make sure that there is a graded system of sanction, make sure that there is a kind of monitoring system. This one is interesting because one of the conclusions from that very empirical literature is that it's not just local self-governance. but it is embedded in other systems, which might be the state or might be market-oriented. So there's literature about digital information, knowledge commons. Benkler especially makes an interesting point. So you have use rights, which is different from property rights, and then things work differently. There are also attempts to apply this to emerging technologies. where it's not about resources, but about risks that you create for others, and I think that might be of relevance to us. And it's a whole discussion on what global is. This is very much open, much more recent, more contested. Ellen Ostrom actually got the Nobel Prize for Economics in 2009 for her work. And I list here a number of themes that come over and over again in this literature that I have read, but just as an amateur. And it's not a central government or a pure market, but what will happen and what is needed is a variety of institutional forms and what she calls polycentric, more or less decentral forms of governance. Other authors talk about the need for... Pretty consonant with that. The need for adaptive governance, and we have that here. All kinds of things are happening. Things are changing. You see it with, let's say, natural resource commons with climate change very much. Situation is different. So what needs to be done is different. So you need some form of evolving adaptive governance. Other points that are made is, and especially for global commons, and most of it is related to natural resources, but it's difficult to do proper governance because we have very limited insights into how these systems really precisely work. So with the small local commons, and that's a point by Eleanor Ostrom, Often, people themselves have a very good view on how it works. That's why, let's say, indigenous knowledge is very important for proper governance. But for the global systems, we do not have that knowledge. So it's important to invest in science in order to understand how the system works, how it works for the users, and how it works for affected people. outside people. And the point that you see often made is integrate scientific analysis with broadly based deliberation. So it's not pure analysis, but it must be integrated with democratic deliberation on what to do. And another theme that comes up all the time is the notion of complexity. This is an example from anthropology, from the Subax in Bali. There are other books with a beautiful title, Priests and Programmers. And the point is that running the rice fields in a certain area in Bali is a very elaborate religion-based system run by priests. And what actually happens is that this is a non-linear dynamic system of water management and they manage it through the religious rituals such that you have the best results because there are differences of interest between people who are higher up in the stream and who are downstream. That must be carefully managed. And this whole book tells how it works. So they did even simulations. That's why these priests are actually programmers and designers of this governance. And similar notions you find in diffusion of innovations. So there's a lot of tendency also in the literature that Bill mentioned to look at the invention. So Kuhn. and that is inspired by Kuhn, you look at the invention. But most of the innovation is after the invention and what happens next. And this is actually focused on such idea for open source software. A very nice book. But the notion that these are non-linear complex systems is basically everywhere. And from there, you have this idea of adaptive, decentral governance. So to sum up, science takes place more and more in the agra of society. There was a lot of protest and anxiety on the physicists that engineered the nuclear bomb. And they wanted him to warn the president not to use it. And he refused to do that. During the Cold War, there were, and this was a minority, but still vocal. You had the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists. You had movements like the Book Wash Movement. You can deliberately make systems whereby people will collaboratively, constructively work together to build a democratic world. Any reaction to that? Yeah, I do think that there are various, I think you point that out in your column or in your response. There are certain business models behind it for companies that have all kinds of outside effects that are negative. I think it's not just one global network, but there are many different areas. open source software or Wikipedia that are basically common type of arrangements that keep out certain business models.
